items.readable_text:
Content:
Let [MATH: A] be a [MATH: 2\times 2] symmetric matrix with real entries. As we know, there exists an orthonormal change of variables

Content:
[MATH: \mathbf{x}=P\mathbf{y}]

Content:
that transforms the quadratic form [MATH: \mathbf{x}^TA\mathbf{x}] into the quadratic form [MATH: \mathbf{y}^TD\mathbf{y},] where [MATH: D] is a diagonal matrix.

Content:
The columns of the matrix [MATH: P] are the (normalized) unit eigenvectors of [MATH: A,] which are mutually orthogonal. These are called the principal axes of the quadratic form.

Content:
Let's use this knowledge to find out which curve is defined by the equation

Content:
[MATH: 6x_1^2+4x_1x_2+3x_2^2= 14,]

Content:
and see the geometric interpretation of the principal axes.

Content:
If we plot our curve using a graphical calculator, we obtain the following:

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/34cef09ac88b98d6a2ae6351d0835a47]

Content:
It looks like an ellipse. Let's now find our coordinate system, in which the equation of the curve will be the simplest.

Content:
First, we consider the corresponding quadratic form

Content:
[MATH: Q(\mathbf{x})={\color{blue}6}x_1^2+{\color{red}4}x_1x_2+{\color{blue}3}x_2^2,]

Content:
which we reduce to its canonical (diagonal) form.

Content:
So, we write down the matrix of [MATH: Q(\mathbf{x}) \mathbin{:}]

Content:
[MATH: [6|2; 2|3]]

Content:
Next, we find the eigenvalues of [MATH: A\mathbin{:}]

Content:
[MATH: |A − λI||= 0;|6 − λ|2; 2|3 − λ||= 0; λ^{2} − 9λ + 14|= 0; λ|= 7, 2]

Content:
Now, let's find the principal axes of the curve.

Content:
- Seeking a non-zero solution of [MATH: (A-7I)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}] gives the eigenvector [MATH: [2; 1]] Dividing [MATH: \mathbf{v}_1] by its norm [MATH: \| \mathbf{v}_1 \| = \sqrt{5},] we get
[MATH: [2; 1]]
- Seeking a non-zero solution of [MATH: (A-2I)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}] gives the eigenvector [MATH: [− 1; 2]] Dividing [MATH: \mathbf{v}_2] by its norm [MATH: \| \mathbf{v}_2 \| = \sqrt{5},] we get
[MATH: [− 1; 2]]

Content:
Therefore, the principal axes of our quadratic form (and the corresponding curve) are

Content:
[MATH: \qquad] [MATH: [2; 1]] and [MATH: [− 1; 2]]

Content:
Notice that in the diagram below, the principal axes correspond to the axes [MATH: y_1] and [MATH: y_2.]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/985b65a4dfd49288dfa8229ce19ed99b]

Content:
In the new coordinate system, our quadratic form can be reduced to

Content:
[MATH: 7y_1^2 + 2y_2^2.]

Content:
Therefore, the curve has the following equation:

Content:
[MATH: 7y_{1}^{2} + 2y_{2}^{2}|= 14; (y_{1}^{2})/((sqrt(2))^{2}) + (y_{2}^{2})/((sqrt(7))^{2})|= 1]

Content:
This is an ellipse with semiaxes [MATH: \sqrt2] and [MATH: \sqrt{7}.]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
The principal axes of a curve define a coordinate system in which the curve can be represented by its (simplest) canonical equation.

Our curve is a hyperbola. This curve will have the canonical equation of the form

[MATH: \dfrac{x^2}{a^2} - \dfrac{y^2}{b^2} = 1]

if one axis passes through the vertices of the hyperbola and the other axis is the perpendicular bisector of the segment connecting the two vertices.

sections.normalized_html: Which curve is defined by the equation [MATH: 6x_1^2+8x_1x_2-9x_2^2= 70?]
sections.readable_text: Which curve is defined by the equation [MATH: 6x_1^2+8x_1x_2-9x_2^2= 70?]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
Consider the quadratic form [MATH: Q(\mathbf{x})=6x_1^2+8x_1x_2-9x_2^2.] To determine the curve defined by the given equation, we reduce [MATH: Q(\mathbf{x})] to its canonical (diagonal) form.

First, we write down the matrix of [MATH: Q(\mathbf{x}),] which is

[MATH: [6|4; 4|− 9]]

Next, we find the eigenvalues of [MATH: A\mathbin{:}]

[MATH: |A − λI||= 0;|6 − λ|4; 4|− 9 − λ||= 0; λ^{2} + 3λ − 70|= 0; λ|= 7, − 10]

So, our quadratic form can be reduced to [MATH: 7y_1^2 -10 y_2^2.]

In the new variables, the curve has the following equation:

[MATH: 7y_{1}^{2} − 10y_{2}^{2}|= 70; (y_{1}^{2})/(10) − (y_{2}^{2})/(7)|= 1; (y_{1}^{2})/((sqrt(10))^{2}) − (y_{2}^{2})/((sqrt(7))^{2})|= 1]

This is a hyperbola with semiaxes [MATH: \sqrt{10}] and [MATH: \sqrt{7}.]

items.title: Some Special Cases

sections.normalized_html: In some special cases, a quadratic equation might generate a degenerate (real) curve or even an empty set.
sections.readable_text: In some special cases, a quadratic equation might generate a degenerate (real) curve or even an empty set.

sections.normalized_html: • For example, consider the quadratic equation [MATH: -3x_1^2+8x_1x_2+3x_2^2 = 0.] Reducing the left-hand side to the canonical form, we obtain [MATH: 5y_1^2 - 5y_2^2 = 0] which represents two intersecting lines [MATH: y_1 = y_2] and [MATH: y_1 = -y_2.]
sections.readable_text:
- For example, consider the quadratic equation [MATH: -3x_1^2+8x_1x_2+3x_2^2 = 0.]
Reducing the left-hand side to the canonical form, we obtain
[MATH: 5y_1^2 - 5y_2^2 = 0]
which represents two intersecting lines [MATH: y_1 = y_2] and [MATH: y_1 = -y_2.]

sections.normalized_html:

items.title: Finding the Principal Axes of a Quadratic Plane Curve Given the Corresponding Eigenvalues

sections.normalized_html: Consider the matrix [MATH: [2|1; 1|2]] and the quadratic curve [MATH: \mathbf{x}^T \! A \mathbf{x} = 1.] Given that [MATH: A] has eigenvalues [MATH: \lambda_1=3] and [MATH: \lambda_2=1,] find the principal axes of the curve.
sections.readable_text: Consider the matrix [MATH: [2|1; 1|2]] and the quadratic curve [MATH: \mathbf{x}^T \! A \mathbf{x} = 1.] Given that [MATH: A] has eigenvalues [MATH: \lambda_1=3] and [MATH: \lambda_2=1,] find the principal axes of the curve.

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
Notice that [MATH: A] is symmetric. The principal axes of the curve

[MATH: \mathbf{x}^T \! A \mathbf{x} = 1]

are the vectors that give an orthonormal eigenvector basis for [MATH: A.] Let's now find these eigenvectors.

  • For [MATH: \lambda_1=3,] we have [MATH: A − 3I|= [2|1; 1|2] − 3[1|0; 0|1] = [− 1|1; 1|− 1].] Seeking a non-zero solution of [MATH: (A-3I)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}] gives the eigenvector [MATH: [1; 1]] Dividing [MATH: \mathbf{v}_1] by its norm [MATH: \| \mathbf{v}_1 \| = \sqrt{2},] we get [MATH: [1; 1]]

  • For [MATH: \lambda_2=1,] we have [MATH: A − 1I|= [− 2|2; 2|1] − 1[1|0; 0|1] = [1|1; 1|1].] Seeking a non-zero solution of [MATH: (A-I)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}] gives the eigenvector [MATH: [− 1; 1]] Dividing [MATH: \mathbf{v}_2] by its norm [MATH: \| \mathbf{v}_2 \| = \sqrt{2},] we get [MATH: [− 1; 1]]

Therefore, the principal axes of our curve are

[MATH: \qquad] [MATH: [1; 1]] and [MATH: [− 1; 1]]

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Let [MATH: A] be a [MATH: 2\times 2] symmetric matrix with real entries. As we know, there exists an orthonormal change of variables

Content:
[MATH: \mathbf{x}=P\mathbf{y}]

Content:
that transforms the quadratic form [MATH: \mathbf{x}^TA\mathbf{x}] into the quadratic form [MATH: \mathbf{y}^TD\mathbf{y},] where [MATH: D] is a diagonal matrix.

Content:
The columns of the matrix [MATH: P] are the (normalized) unit eigenvectors of [MATH: A,] which are mutually orthogonal. These are called the principal axes of the quadratic form.

Content:
Let's use this knowledge to find out which curve is defined by the equation

Content:
[MATH: 6x_1^2+4x_1x_2+3x_2^2= 14,]

Content:
and see the geometric interpretation of the principal axes.

Content:
If we plot our curve using a graphical calculator, we obtain the following:

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/34cef09ac88b98d6a2ae6351d0835a47]

Content:
It looks like an ellipse. Let's now find our coordinate system, in which the equation of the curve will be the simplest.

Content:
First, we consider the corresponding quadratic form

Content:
[MATH: Q(\mathbf{x})={\color{blue}6}x_1^2+{\color{red}4}x_1x_2+{\color{blue}3}x_2^2,]

Content:
which we reduce to its canonical (diagonal) form.

Content:
So, we write down the matrix of [MATH: Q(\mathbf{x}) \mathbin{:}]

Content:
[MATH: [6|2; 2|3]]

Content:
Next, we find the eigenvalues of [MATH: A\mathbin{:}]

Content:
[MATH: |A − λI||= 0;|6 − λ|2; 2|3 − λ||= 0; λ^{2} − 9λ + 14|= 0; λ|= 7, 2]

Content:
Now, let's find the principal axes of the curve.

Content:
- Seeking a non-zero solution of [MATH: (A-7I)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}] gives the eigenvector [MATH: [2; 1]] Dividing [MATH: \mathbf{v}_1] by its norm [MATH: \| \mathbf{v}_1 \| = \sqrt{5},] we get
[MATH: [2; 1]]
- Seeking a non-zero solution of [MATH: (A-2I)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}] gives the eigenvector [MATH: [− 1; 2]] Dividing [MATH: \mathbf{v}_2] by its norm [MATH: \| \mathbf{v}_2 \| = \sqrt{5},] we get
[MATH: [− 1; 2]]

Content:
Therefore, the principal axes of our quadratic form (and the corresponding curve) are

Content:
[MATH: \qquad] [MATH: [2; 1]] and [MATH: [− 1; 2]]

Content:
Notice that in the diagram below, the principal axes correspond to the axes [MATH: y_1] and [MATH: y_2.]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/985b65a4dfd49288dfa8229ce19ed99b]

Content:
In the new coordinate system, our quadratic form can be reduced to

Content:
[MATH: 7y_1^2 + 2y_2^2.]

Content:
Therefore, the curve has the following equation:

Content:
[MATH: 7y_{1}^{2} + 2y_{2}^{2}|= 14; (y_{1}^{2})/((sqrt(2))^{2}) + (y_{2}^{2})/((sqrt(7))^{2})|= 1]

Content:
This is an ellipse with semiaxes [MATH: \sqrt2] and [MATH: \sqrt{7}.]

---

Item 2 — Example: Identifying the Principal Axes of a Quadratic Curve Using a Diagram

Example Prompt:
Draw a diagram that depicts the lines representing the principal axes of the quadratic curve shown below.

[IMG: /graphics/fa1f2ef5edfdc2471cf95a125c9702a1]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
The principal axes of a curve define a coordinate system in which the curve can be represented by its (simplest) canonical equation.

Our curve is a hyperbola. This curve will have the canonical equation of the form

[MATH: \dfrac{x^2}{a^2} - \dfrac{y^2}{b^2} = 1]

if one axis passes through the vertices of the hyperbola and the other axis is the perpendicular bisector of the segment connecting the two vertices.

[IMG: /graphics/2503cf232548072ca23d6152156ff107]

Item 5 — Example: Identifying a Quadratic Plane Curve

Example Prompt:
Which curve is defined by the equation [MATH: 6x_1^2+8x_1x_2-9x_2^2= 70?]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Consider the quadratic form [MATH: Q(\mathbf{x})=6x_1^2+8x_1x_2-9x_2^2.] To determine the curve defined by the given equation, we reduce [MATH: Q(\mathbf{x})] to its canonical (diagonal) form.

First, we write down the matrix of [MATH: Q(\mathbf{x}),] which is

[MATH: [6|4; 4|− 9]]

Next, we find the eigenvalues of [MATH: A\mathbin{:}]

[MATH: |A − λI||= 0;|6 − λ|4; 4|− 9 − λ||= 0; λ^{2} + 3λ − 70|= 0; λ|= 7, − 10]

So, our quadratic form can be reduced to [MATH: 7y_1^2 -10 y_2^2.]

In the new variables, the curve has the following equation:

[MATH: 7y_{1}^{2} − 10y_{2}^{2}|= 70; (y_{1}^{2})/(10) − (y_{2}^{2})/(7)|= 1; (y_{1}^{2})/((sqrt(10))^{2}) − (y_{2}^{2})/((sqrt(7))^{2})|= 1]

This is a hyperbola with semiaxes [MATH: \sqrt{10}] and [MATH: \sqrt{7}.]

Item 8 — Tutorial: Some Special Cases

Content:
In some special cases, a quadratic equation might generate a degenerate (real) curve or even an empty set.

Content:
- For example, consider the quadratic equation [MATH: -3x_1^2+8x_1x_2+3x_2^2 = 0.]
Reducing the left-hand side to the canonical form, we obtain
[MATH: 5y_1^2 - 5y_2^2 = 0]
which represents two intersecting lines [MATH: y_1 = y_2] and [MATH: y_1 = -y_2.]

Content:
- Now consider the quadratic equation [MATH: -2x_1^2+8x_1x_2-8x_2^2 = 10.]
Reducing the left-hand side to the canonical form, we obtain
[MATH: - 10y_2^2 =10]
which represents an empty set as the equation [MATH: y_2^2 = -1] does not have any real solution.
- Finally, reducing the left-hand side of [MATH: x_1^2-4x_1x_2+4x_2^2 = 5]
to the canonical form, we obtain
[MATH: 5y_2^2 =5]
which represents a pair of parallel lines [MATH: y_2 = 1] and [MATH: y_2=-1.]
